title: Pituitary and pineal glands and the midline of the brain (medial view)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Location
Front lobe of the pituitary gland, in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone.
Function
Secretes FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, prolactin, and growth hormone, under the control of hypothalamic hormones that reach it through the hypophyseal portal veins.
hy: It develops from the roof of the mouth (Rathke pouch, oral ectoderm), unlike the posterior pituitary, which grows down from the brain.
A pituitary adenoma can press on the optic chiasm above it and cause bitemporal hemianopia. The most common secreting adenoma is a prolactinoma.

rows: Location
Back lobe of the pituitary gland. It is a downward extension of the hypothalamus.
Function
Stores and releases antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin, which are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and carried down their axons.
hy: Loss of antidiuretic hormone causes central diabetes insipidus.

rows: Location
In the midline at the back of the third ventricle, above the superior colliculi.
Function
Secretes melatonin, which helps set the sleep and wake cycle.
hy: A pineal tumor presses on the upper midbrain, causing paralysis of upward gaze (Parinaud syndrome), and can block the cerebral aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus.

rows: Location
Below the thalamus, forming the floor and the lower side walls of the third ventricle.
Function
Keeps the body in balance: temperature, hunger, thirst, the sleep and wake cycle, the autonomic nervous system, and, through the pituitary, the endocrine system.
hy: Lateral nucleus: hunger (a lesion causes loss of appetite). Ventromedial nucleus: fullness (a lesion causes overeating). Anterior nucleus: cooling. Posterior nucleus: heating. Suprachiasmatic nucleus: circadian rhythm.

rows: Location
Egg-shaped mass on each side of the third ventricle.
Function
Relay station for almost all sensory input to the cortex (smell is the exception) and for motor signals from the cerebellum and basal ganglia.
hy: Main relay nuclei: VPL (sensation from the body), VPM (sensation from the face, and taste), lateral geniculate (vision), medial geniculate (hearing), ventral lateral (motor).

rows: Location
Thick band of white matter that arches over the lateral ventricles in the midline. From front to back: rostrum, genu, body, splenium.
Function
Connects matching areas of the two cerebral hemispheres.
Location
Thin sheet in the midline between the corpus callosum above and the fornix below.
Function
Separates the anterior horns of the two lateral ventricles.
Location
Arching bundle of white matter under the corpus callosum, running from the hippocampus to the mammillary body.
Function
Main output pathway of the hippocampus. It is part of the limbic circuit for memory.
Location
One of a pair of small round swellings on the underside of the hypothalamus, behind the pituitary stalk.
Function
Receives the fornix and projects to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. It is part of the limbic circuit for memory.
hy: Damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is due to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most often in alcohol use disorder: confusion, paralysis of eye movements, and ataxia, then memory loss with confabulation.

rows: Location
Uppermost part of the brainstem, between the thalamus and the pons. The cerebral aqueduct runs through it.
Function

Holds the nuclei of the oculomotor and trochlear nerves, the superior and inferior colliculi (visual and auditory reflexes), the substantia nigra, and the red nucleus; the cerebral peduncles carry the descending motor fibers.
hy: Loss of the dopamine-producing neurons of the substantia nigra causes Parkinson disease.
A midbrain stroke that involves the oculomotor nerve fibers and the cerebral peduncle causes an oculomotor palsy on the same side with weakness of the opposite side of the body (Weber syndrome).

rows: Location
Middle part of the brainstem, between the midbrain and the medulla, in front of the cerebellum.
Function
Holds the nuclei of the trigeminal, abducens, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves, and relays signals from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum through the middle cerebellar peduncles.
hy: Correcting a low blood sodium too quickly can destroy myelin in the center of the pons (osmotic demyelination syndrome), causing paralysis and, at worst, locked-in syndrome.

rows: Location
Lowest part of the brainstem. It continues as the spinal cord at the foramen magnum.
Function
Holds the centers that control breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure and the nuclei of the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and hypoglossal nerves. Most corticospinal fibers cross in its pyramids.
hy: When the cerebellar tonsils are pushed down through the foramen magnum they compress the medulla, which can stop breathing.

Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery damages its lateral part (lateral medullary, or Wallenberg, syndrome): difficulty swallowing, hoarseness, vertigo, and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the same side of the face and the opposite side of the body.

rows: Location
Posterior cranial fossa, behind the pons and medulla and below the tentorium cerebelli.
Function
Coordinates movement, balance, and posture by comparing the movement that was intended with the movement that is taking place.
hy: Cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion. A lesion of a hemisphere causes limb ataxia and intention tremor, with a tendency to fall toward that side; a lesion of the vermis causes a wide-based gait and unsteadiness of the trunk.

rows: Location
Medial surface of the hemisphere, arching just above the corpus callosum.
Function
Part of the limbic system: emotion, motivation, and attention.
hy: In subfalcine herniation the cingulate gyrus is pushed under the falx cerebri and can compress the anterior cerebral artery.

rows: Location
Stalk that runs from the floor of the hypothalamus down to the pituitary gland.
Function
Carries the axons from the hypothalamus to the posterior pituitary and the portal veins to the anterior pituitary.
hy: When the stalk is cut or compressed, the other anterior pituitary hormones typically fall while prolactin rises, because dopamine from the hypothalamus no longer holds it back.
